title: Workplace Gossip When It Helps and When It Hurts
paragraphs: Gossip is often seen as a bad habit, especially at work. But experts say that talking about colleagues who are not present is not always harmful, and in some cases it can even be useful.

According to Stephen Lee, an assistant professor of management at Washington State University, gossip is often a sign of a problem that an organization has overlooked. For example, warning a coworker about a difficult person can protect them and build goodwill. Lee also points out that venting to a trusted colleague after a frustrating experience can help people manage their emotions. Gossip can even be positive, such as praising someone who is not in the room.

Rebecca Greenbaum, a professor of human resource management at Rutgers University who studies workplace gossip, agrees that it can increase cooperation and a sense of belonging. People sometimes share sensitive information to show that they care, or to learn who they can trust. Telling a colleague that someone is in a bad mood, for instance, can help them adjust their behavior.

However, gossip can easily backfire. It can damage the reputation of the person being discussed, as well as that of the person spreading it. Mariah Humbert, an etiquette consultant in New York, warns that constant negative talk puts a person's trust and credibility at risk. Humbert suggests responding to gossip politely without joining in, and having a few neutral topics ready, such as weekend plans or hobbies, to change the subject.

Bev Vitali of the Tennessee Nonprofit Network recalls spending a lot of time gossiping when rumors of layoffs spread at a former job, which made her less productive. She says that if you learn about serious behavior, it is better to report it to someone who can act, such as human resources. For simple venting, she recommends talking to someone outside the company.

So how can you tell if gossip is harmful? Greenbaum suggests asking yourself why you are sharing it, whether the person deserves it, and how serious the information is. Feeling guilty afterward may be a sign that you have gone against your own values.
